newsitem.title: CANADA: Bombardier buys rest of plane maker de Havilland.
newsitem.headline: Bombardier buys rest of plane maker de Havilland.

text.p: Bombardier Inc said on Tuesday that it acquired the Ontario government's 49 percent stake in de Havilland, bringing its ownership of the Toronto-based plane maker to 100 percent.
Montreal-based Bombardier paid C$49 million ($36 million) for the province's stake.
In 1992, Bombardier and Ontario acquired the then ailing turboprop aircraft maker from Boeing Co for C$100 million ($74 million).
Bombardier paid C$51 million ($38 million) for its original 51 percent holding in de Havilland and had until Jan. 31 to buy the provincial government's stake.
Bombardier said that under the transaction, final aircraft assembly would continue at de Havilland and the plane maker would participate in Bombardier's aerospace programs.
De Havilland was founded in Canada in 1928 and has 5,600 employees. It makes the de Havilland family of 37, 50 and 70-passenger twin-engined Dash 8 turboprop planes.

In the past five years, Bombardier integrated de Havilland into its own growing aerospace manufacturing operations. De Havilland currently completes final assembly of the Bombardier Global Express business jet and designs and manufactures the wing for Bombardier's Learjet 45 small-sized business jet.

De Havilland is also headquarters for Bombardier's Regional Aircraft Division, which is responsible for the marketing, sales, contracts and product support of the Dash 8 and 50-seat Canadair Regional Jet.

Bombardier is an aerospace, rail transportation and motorized consumer products maker, with manufacturing plants in Canada, the United States, Mexico, the United Kingdom and Europe. It has C$7 billion ($5.2 billion) in annual sales and 40,000 employees worldwide.
Bombardier shares were down C10 cents to C$25,10 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
